title: Work as practice
hookLine: the Buddha taught farmers, traders, kings and servants where they were
tomorrow: what makes a job honest: what you sell, or how you sell it?

lines: WHAT DO YOU DO ALL DAY?
I PLOW AND SOW. DO YOU?
cards: On a new job, someone always asks what you actually do all day. A farmer once put that question to the Buddha. It's sowing season.
A brahmin named Bharadvaja has his plows out in the field, and food is being handed out to the workers. The Buddha walks up with his bowl and stands there. The farmer looks him over.
I plow and sow, he says, and when I've plowed and sown, I eat. You should plow and sow too, and then eat. A fair point, from a man with dirt on his hands.
And the Buddha says: I too plow and sow, and then I eat. The farmer squints. I don't see your yoke, or your plow, or your ox.

teach.h: FAITH THE SEED, WISDOM THE PLOW.
teach.b: So the Buddha answers in the farmer's own language. Faith is the seed, he says. Discipline is the rain.
Wisdom is my yoke and plow. Conscience is the pole, the mind is the strap, mindfulness my plowshare and goad. Effort is my ox, pulling toward freedom without turning back.
That's the whole move. He doesn't drag the farmer out of the field to teach him.

teach.h: HE TEACHES IN THE FARMER'S FIELD.
teach.b: He walks into the field and teaches in plows and oxen. And it cuts the other way too. If the path can be described as farming, a farmer's day can carry the path.
The plowshare is mindfulness. The straight furrow is attention that doesn't wander off. Work as practice doesn't mean quitting your job for a temple.
It means the barista, the nurse, the coder and the mat cutter bring the same tools to the task in front of them: a steady mind, honest effort, attention on the next cut. One more detail.
The farmer is so moved that he offers a big bowl of milk-rice.
The Buddha declines it. He won't take food earned by reciting verses. Even in the field, he keeps the teaching from becoming a sale.

how: In Zen monasteries, daily work such as cooking and cleaning (samu) is treated as practice, and lay Buddhists bring mindfulness to their jobs in the same spirit.

o: working extra hours as a kind of offering
leaving your job to live in a monastery
bringing the path's tools to your daily work

games.q: the Buddha's plowing — tap the pairs.
p: the ox that doesn't turn back

s: in Buddhism, real practice only happens away from work
the Buddha told a farmer he plows too, and taught him in plows and oxen.
the Buddha turned down the farmer's milk-rice
he wouldn't take food earned by reciting verses.
when the farmer said to plow and sow, the Buddha said he doesn't
he said he does: faith is his seed, wisdom his yoke and plow.

games.q: your friend is a barista and says her job is "just making coffee," nothing spiritual. what fits work as practice?
o: each cup can get her full attention; the job itself can carry practice.
she should find a calmer job first, and start practicing after that.
work can't be practice; she should meditate on her breaks instead.
games.why: the Buddha met a farmer in his own field and described his practice as plowing. the work in front of you can carry the path.

practice: Pick up one small task within reach: fold a blanket, wipe a screen, line up the pens. Do only that, slowly, with your whole attention on your hands, like a furrow you're keeping straight.
When the mind wanders off, bring it back to the hands.

wordCard.voice: Work as practice: bringing the path's tools, mindfulness, effort and a steady mind, to the work in front of you.

orig.note: Pali: kasi, plowing or farming, as in the farmer's name in the sutta, Kasibharadvaja.

carryVoice: Keep this one: where you are, in the field you're already standing in. One of fifty, and the new stretch has begun.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 1.4, Kasibharadvaja Sutta (I too plow and sow: faith the seed, discipline the rain, wisdom yoke and plow, conscience the pole, mind the strap, mindfulness plowshare and goad, effort the beast of burden; the Buddha declines food 'chanted over with verses')
Samyutta Nikaya 7.11, Kasi Sutta (the same encounter)
